learn.title: Comparative adjectives
learn.html:
They compare two people or things. Before the second element goes than: Texting is quicker and easier than calling.

TypeRuleExamples
Short adjectiveadjective + -erquick → quicker, slow → slower
Ends in -eonly add -rnice → nicer
Consonant + -yy → -iereasy → easier
Vowel + consonant (not w)double the consonantbig → bigger
Long adjectivemore / less + adjectivemore personal, less expensive, more interesting
Irregulargood → better, bad → worseVideo calls are better than phone calls.

With fun use more: Texting is more fun than calling. To qualify a comparison, use a lot / much / a little / a bit + comparative: Email is a lot faster than regular mail.

watch.wrong: Texting is more quick than calling.
Cards are more personal that e-cards.
watch.right: Cards are more personal than e-cards.
watch.why: The word used to compare is than, not that.

watch.right: This spam is worse than yesterday's.

watch.wrong: Video calls are more better than texts.
watch.right: Video calls are better than texts.
watch.why: Better is already a comparative, so don't add more.

learn.title: as … as, the same as, different from
learn.html:
Besides -er / more … than, you can say that two things are the same or different.

StructureMeaningExample
as + adjective + asequally … asA text is as quick as a call.
not as + adjective + asless … thanTexting is not as personal as a letter.
the same asidentical toMy phone is the same as yours.
different fromnot the same asA video call is different from a phone call.

Not as … as and less … than mean almost the same: Texting isn't as personal as calling = Texting is less personal than calling.

watch.wrong: Email is not as fast than a text.
watch.right: Email is not as fast as a text.
watch.why: With as … , close with as, not than.

watch.wrong: My phone is same as yours.
watch.right: My phone is the same as yours.
watch.why: The article "the" is missing before same.

watch.wrong: Video calls are different than phone calls.
watch.right: Video calls are different from phone calls.
watch.why: More formal and more precise: different from.

watch.wrong: He is as tall like his father.
watch.right: He is as tall as his father.
watch.why: To say equal to, use as … as, not "like".

learn.title: More, less and fewer
learn.html:
You can also compare with nouns and verbs. Fewer and less are the opposite of more. After them comes than.

With…StructureExample
Countable noun (plural)more / fewer + nounI get more calls than you. You get fewer calls than I do.
Uncountable nounmore / less + nounI spend more time on the phone. You spend less time on the phone.
Verbverb + more / less + thanShe talks more than he does. He talks less than she does.

After than you can end with an auxiliary: than you do, than he does, than I did.

watch.wrong: I get less calls than you.
watch.right: I get fewer calls than you.

watch.wrong: She has fewer money than me.
watch.right: She has less money than me.

watch.wrong: He talks more that she does.
watch.right: He talks more than she does.

watch.wrong: I text more than you do it.
watch.right: I text more than you do.
watch.why: Do replaces the verb; don't add it.

learn.title: Using just
learn.html:
Just has several very common uses in conversation:

UseMeaningExample
Softening a commandmore polite, less directJust a minute. I've got another call.
Playing something down"only", "nothing more"I was just calling to say hi.
A moment agojust now + past simpleI just got your message.

It goes before the main verb (I just got) or before the phrase it softens (Just wait a second).

watch.why: To soften a request, just goes at the beginning.
Just goes before the main verb.

watch.wrong: I am calling only just to say hi.
watch.right: I'm just calling to say hi.
watch.why: Only and just aren't used together.

learn.title: Interrupting and resuming the conversation
learn.html:
To interrupt (pause) a conversation:

  • Just a minute. / Just a second.
  • Excuse me just a second.
  • I'm sorry. Hold on (a second).
  • Could / Can you hold on a second?

To resume afterward:

  • What were you saying? / You were saying?
  • Where were we? / What were we talking about?

A: Juan and I went to a fancy restaurant last night and… B: Oh, just a minute. I've got another call. … Sorry. So, what were you saying?

learn.title: Strategy: writing an article with pros and cons
learn.html:
A pros and cons article has 4 parts:

  1. Introduction: introduce the topic. Video calling is becoming more and more popular.
  2. Advantages: reasons in favor. It's fun to video call a friend you don't see often.
  3. Disadvantages: reasons against, with However, … / On the other hand, …
  4. Conclusion: your point of view with I think … / In my opinion, …

Use comparatives (quicker than, more personal than) and more / less / fewer to support your ideas.

write.prompt: Write an article of 120 to 180 words about the advantages and disadvantages of a form of communication (for example, video calls or text messages). Include: an introduction, at least two advantages, at least one disadvantage with However or On the other hand, and a conclusion with In my opinion.
checklist: At least 3 correct comparatives (quicker than, more personal than)
One sentence with fewer or less used correctly
However / On the other hand in the disadvantages
In my opinion or I think in the conclusion
write.model:
Video calls: good or bad?

Nowadays many people use video calls to talk with family and colleagues. They are very popular, but are they always the best choice?

One advantage is that video calls are more personal than text messages. You can see the other person's face, so it is easier to understand their feelings. Another advantage is that they are quicker than writing long emails, and they are cheaper than traveling to a meeting. With video calls, we spend less money and fewer hours on the road.

However, there are some disadvantages. The internet connection is sometimes slower than we need, and the image can freeze. On the other hand, a text message is easier to send when you are busy. Also, video calls can be more tiring than normal phone calls because you must look at the screen all the time.

In my opinion, video calls are the best way to keep in touch with people who live far away, but I think we should use messages for short, simple things.

write.prompt: Write a message of 120 to 180 words to a friend who lives far away. Tell them how you keep in touch and compare two ways of communicating (for example, texting and video calls). Use as … as, more / less / fewer and a just to soften something, and suggest a call.
checklist: One sentence with not as … as
One sentence with more, less or fewer + noun
One just used to soften (Just call me…)
A question to suggest a video call
write.model:
Hi Laura,

How are you? I miss you a lot! I want to tell you how I keep in touch with my friends now that we live in different cities. I mostly send text messages because they are quicker than calls, and I can answer when I have time. But texting is not as fun as talking to someone. Video calls are more personal than messages, and I can see your face and your new haircut!

These days I have less free time than before, so I have fewer chances to call. I have more work and more homework than last year, so I usually write short messages at lunch. Writing is easier than calling, but it is not as warm as hearing your voice. Just call me if you have a problem, and I will always answer.

What about you? Do you prefer texting or calling? Why don't we have a video call this Sunday afternoon? I can make some coffee, and you can tell me about your new job.

Hugs,
Marta

reading.title: Is texting better than calling?
reading.intro: Read about a one-week experiment and answer.
paragraphs: Technology gives us many ways to keep in touch. My grandmother sends regular mail, my parents prefer phone calls, and my friends and I use instant messaging all day. But which way is better? Last month I tried an experiment: for one week, I used a different kind of communication every day.

On Monday I sent a text to my best friend. Texting is quicker and easier than calling, and I received an answer in two minutes. However, it is less personal. I couldn't hear her voice, so I didn't know if she was happy or tired. On Tuesday I tried a video call with my cousin in Canada. It was more fun than a text because I could see his face and his new dog. On the other hand, the connection was slow, and we had to repeat many things.

On Wednesday I wrote a real letter to my grandmother. It was harder than I thought, because I write fewer letters than anyone I know. I also spend less time at home these days, so it was difficult to find a stamp. But a week later she called me and said it was the best surprise of the year. A real card is more personal than an e-card, and she kept my letter on her kitchen table.

By Friday I had an answer to my question. Video calls are better than texts when you want to see someone you miss, but they are not as convenient as messages, because both people need time. Texts are perfect for quick plans. Letters are slower than anything, but they are the most special. In my opinion, there isn't one best way. The best way is simply to keep in touch, and I'm going to use all of them: a text for plans, a video call for my cousin and a letter, just once a month, for my grandmother.

listening.intro: Listen to the phone call between Marco and Ana. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Hi, Ana! It's Marco. I was just calling to ask about Saturday.
Oh, hi, Marco! Are you talking about Sofía's party?
Yes. I sent you a text yesterday, but you didn't answer.
Sorry! I get more messages than I can read. My inbox is full of spam.
I know. I get fewer texts than you, but I never check my voice mail.
Oh, just a second. I've got another call. ... Sorry about that. So, what were you saying?
I was asking about the gift. I think a card is nicer than a gift card.
I agree. A real card is more personal than an e-card.
Great. And can you bring the cake? I'll bring the music.
Sure. But calling is slower than texting, so next time send me a message.
Ha! Texting is quicker, but I think a call is more fun. See you Saturday at six!
